subchapters.title: Motion in one dimension
subchapters.theory: One-dimensional motion describes an object's position along a single coordinate axis. Position is specified by x(t); velocity is the rate of change of position and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
key_points: Velocity is a vector; speed is its magnitude.
Average velocity uses displacement, not total distance.
Acceleration can be opposite to velocity.
derivations: Define position x(t).
Differentiate x(t) with respect to time to obtain velocity.
Differentiate velocity to obtain acceleration.
subchapters.examples: If x = 4t^2, v = dx/dt = 8t and a = 8 m s^-2.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Motion in one dimension?
options: Velocity is a vector; speed is its magnitude.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Motion in one dimension.

revision: Velocity is a vector; speed is its magnitude.
Average velocity uses displacement, not total distance.
Acceleration can be opposite to velocity.

subchapters.title: Position, distance and displacement
subchapters.theory: Position gives the location relative to an origin. Distance is the total path length and is a scalar. Displacement is the directed change in position and is a vector. Distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
key_points: Distance is path dependent.
Displacement depends only on initial and final positions.
For a closed trip, displacement can be zero while distance is non-zero.
derivations: Mark initial and final positions.
Calculate final minus initial coordinate for displacement.
Add all path segments for distance.
subchapters.examples: A runner completing one 400 m lap has distance 400 m but displacement 0.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Position, distance and displacement?
options: Distance is path dependent.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Position, distance and displacement.

revision: Displacement depends only on initial and final positions.
For a closed trip, displacement can be zero while distance is non-zero.

subchapters.title: Speed and velocity
subchapters.theory: Speed is the scalar rate of change of distance; velocity is the vector rate of change of displacement. Instantaneous velocity is dx/dt, while instantaneous speed is the magnitude of velocity.
key_points: Average speed = total distance/total time.
Average velocity = displacement/total time.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity.
derivations: Calculate total path and total time for average speed.
Use net displacement for average velocity.
For instantaneous values use derivatives.
subchapters.examples: A particle moving at constant speed around a circle has nonzero acceleration because its velocity direction changes.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Speed and velocity?
options: Average speed = total distance/total time.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Speed and velocity.

revision: Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity.

subchapters.title: Acceleration
subchapters.theory: Acceleration measures how rapidly velocity changes. It may change the magnitude, direction, or both. Uniform acceleration means constant acceleration vector.
key_points: Acceleration is a vector.
Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down; direction of velocity matters.
For constant acceleration, kinematic equations apply.
derivations: Find the change in velocity vector.
Divide by time interval for average acceleration.
Use dv/dt for instantaneous acceleration.
subchapters.examples: Velocity changing from 10 to 20 m/s in 5 s gives average acceleration 2 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Acceleration?
options: Acceleration is a vector.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Acceleration.

revision: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down; direction of velocity matters.
For constant acceleration, kinematic equations apply.

subchapters.title: Equations of motion
subchapters.theory: For constant acceleration, the kinematic equations connect displacement, initial velocity, final velocity and time. They follow directly from a = dv/dt and the definition of velocity.
key_points: v = u + at.
derivations: Integrate a = dv/dt for v = u + at.
Use v = dx/dt and integrate velocity to obtain displacement.
Eliminate time to obtain v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
subchapters.examples: From rest with a = 2 m/s^2 for 5 s: v = 10 m/s and s = 25 m.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Equations of motion?
options: v = u + at.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Equations of motion.

subchapters.title: Motion graphs
subchapters.theory: Graphs provide a visual description of motion. The slope of an x-t graph is velocity; the slope of a v-t graph is acceleration; area under a v-t graph gives displacement.
key_points: Slope of x-t = velocity.
Slope of v-t = acceleration.
Area under v-t = displacement.
derivations: Identify the graph axes.
Use slope for rate quantities.
Use area under v-t or a-t graphs for accumulated quantities.
subchapters.examples: A horizontal v-t line represents constant velocity; its area is v×t.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Motion graphs?
options: Slope of x-t = velocity.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Motion graphs.

revision: Core formula: slope of x-t graph

subchapters.title: Projectile motion
subchapters.theory: Projectile motion is two-dimensional motion under uniform gravitational acceleration when air resistance is neglected. Horizontal motion has constant velocity, while vertical motion has acceleration −g.
key_points: u_x = u cosθ and u_y = u sinθ.
Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g for same-level projection and landing.
Range R = u^2 sin2θ/g; maximum at 45°.
derivations: Resolve initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
Use y = u_y t − 1/2gt^2 and set y=0 for flight time.
Use x = u_x T to obtain range.
subchapters.examples: For u=20 m/s, θ=30°, g=10 m/s², T=2 s.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Projectile motion?
options: u_x = u cosθ and u_y = u sinθ.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Projectile motion.

revision: u_x = u cosθ and u_y = u sinθ.
Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g for same-level projection and landing.
Range R = u^2 sin2θ/g; maximum at 45°.

subchapters.title: Relative motion
subchapters.theory: Relative velocity describes motion as seen from another moving reference object. The relative velocity of A with respect to B is the vector difference v_A − v_B.
key_points: Relative velocity is frame dependent.
For collinear motion use signed velocities.
For perpendicular velocities use vector addition/subtraction.
derivations: Choose the reference object.
Assign consistent velocity vectors.
Subtract the reference velocity from the object's velocity.
subchapters.examples: If two cars move in the same direction at 20 and 15 m/s, the faster car has relative speed 5 m/s.

options: Relative velocity is frame dependent.
